claim: Piezo1 is a stretch-gated ion channel required for mechanosensation in many organ systems.
source: Piezo1 is a stretch-gated ion channel required for mechanosensation in many organ systems.
evidence: This is a general statement about Piezo1 function that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Recent findings suggest that Piezo1 is a sensor of microbial single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) rather than mechanical force.
source: Recent findings point to a new role for Piezo1 in the gut, suggesting that it is a sensor of microbial single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) rather than mechanical force.
evidence: This claim references prior published findings (Sugisawa et al., 2020) that the authors are attempting to replicate.

claim: Fecal extracts and ssRNA can stimulate calcium influx in certain cell lines.
source: While we observe that fecal extracts and ssRNA can stimulate calcium influx in certain cell lines, this response is independent of Piezo1.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript showing responses in specific cell lines.

claim: The calcium response to fecal extracts and ssRNA is independent of Piezo1.
source: While we observe that fecal extracts and ssRNA can stimulate calcium influx in certain cell lines, this response is independent of Piezo1.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using Piezo1-KO cells and comparing transfected vs untransfected cells.

claim: Sterilized dietary extracts devoid of gut biome RNA show similar cell line-specific stimulatory activity to fecal extracts.
source: Additionally, sterilized dietary extracts devoid of gut biome RNA show similar cell line-specific stimulatory activity to fecal extracts.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging experiments comparing dietary and fecal extracts.

claim: Piezo1 is not a receptor for ssRNA in the gut.
source: Together, our data highlight potential confounds inherent to gut-derived extracts, exclude Piezo1 as a receptor for ssRNA in the gut, and support a dedicated role for Piezo channels in mechanosensing.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the negative results from multiple experimental approaches in the study.

claim: Piezo channels have a dedicated role in mechanosensing.
source: Together, our data highlight potential confounds inherent to gut-derived extracts, exclude Piezo1 as a receptor for ssRNA in the gut, and support a dedicated role for Piezo channels in mechanosensing.
evidence: This is supported by the authors' data and established knowledge about Piezo channel function.

claim: Piezo proteins transduce changes in plasma membrane tension into electrical current.
source: Piezo proteins are mechanically gated ion channels that transduce changes in plasma membrane tension into electrical current (Ridone et al., 2019; Szczot et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: There are two members in the mammalian Piezo family: Piezo1 and Piezo2.
source: There are two members in the mammalian Piezo family: Piezo1 and Piezo2 (Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: Piezo1 is expressed in many tissues, including the cardiovascular, hematopoietic, and skeletal systems.
source: Piezo1 is expressed in many tissues, including the cardiovascular, hematopoietic, and skeletal systems (Jiang et al., 2021; Li et al., 2014; Retailleau et al., 2015; Rode et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Piezo1 mediates the mechanical sensing of fluid flow.
source: Specifically, Piezo1 mediates the mechanical sensing of fluid flow and is required for normal development and function of lymph and blood vessels (Li et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020; Nonomura et al., 2018; Ranade et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Piezo1 is required for normal development and function of lymph and blood vessels.
source: Specifically, Piezo1 mediates the mechanical sensing of fluid flow and is required for normal development and function of lymph and blood vessels (Li et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2020; Nonomura et al., 2018; Ranade et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many blood cell types depend on Piezo1 for shear force sensing and volume regulation.
source: Additionally, many blood cell types depend on Piezo1 for shear force sensing and volume regulation (Cahalan et al., 2015; Cinar et al., 2015; Faucherre et al., 2014; Solis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vascular functions of Piezo1 are evident in the clinical manifestation of Piezo1 mutations in humans.
source: These vascular functions are particularly evident in the clinical manifestation of Piezo1 mutations in humans (Albuisson et al., 2013; Bae et al., 2013; Fotiou et al., 2015; Glogowska et al., 2017; Lukacs et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Piezo1 regulates the formation and maintenance of bone and cartilage through mechanical load sensing.
source: Piezo1 also regulates the formation and maintenance of bone and cartilage through mechanical load sensing (Hendrickx et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Piezo1 functions as a mechanosensor in neural stem cells and certain epithelial and mesenchymal cell types.
source: In other organ systems, the role of Piezo1 is currently less well-defined, but it is known to function as a mechanosensor in neural stem cells and certain epithelial and mesenchymal cell types (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Martins et al., 2016; Miyamoto et al., 2014; Pathak et al., 2014; Sugimoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Piezo2 is expressed at its highest levels in the somatosensory system, vagal-nodose complex, and specialized epithelial cells.
source: By contrast, the homologous Piezo2 is expressed at its highest levels in the somatosensory system, vagal-nodose complex, and specialized epithelial cells (Chiu et al., 2014; Kupari et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2017; Usoskin et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Piezo2 is responsible for detecting gentle touch, vibration, and proprioception in mice and humans.
source: Piezo2 is responsible for detecting gentle touch, vibration, and proprioception in mice and humans (Chesler et al., 2016; Ranade et al., 2014a; Woo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many extrinsic factors can influence Piezo mechanosensitivity, including membrane tension, membrane voltage, cytoskeletal integrity, extracellular matrix contact, cyclic adenosine monophosphate signaling, and phosphatidylinositol second messenger pathways.
source: Many extrinsic factors can influence Piezo mechanosensitivity, including membrane tension, membrane voltage, cytoskeletal integrity, extracellular matrix contact, cyclic adenosine monophosphate signaling, and phosphatidylinositol second messenger pathways (Borbiro et al., 2015; Dubin et al., 2012; Gaub and Müller, 2017; Moroni et al., 2018; Narayanan et al., 2018; Romero et al., 2019; Romero et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: High-throughput drug screens have generated synthetic small molecules called Yoda1, Jedi1, and Jedi2, which act as allosteric modulators of Piezo1.
source: Indeed, high-throughput drug screens have generated the synthetic small molecules called Yoda1, Jedi1, and Jedi2, which act as allosteric modulators of Piezo1 by stabilizing its open conformation (Botello-Smith et al., 2019; Syeda et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Yoda1, Jedi1, and Jedi2 stabilize the open conformation of Piezo1.
source: Indeed, high-throughput drug screens have generated the synthetic small molecules called Yoda1, Jedi1, and Jedi2, which act as allosteric modulators of Piezo1 by stabilizing its open conformation (Botello-Smith et al., 2019; Syeda et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A recent study provided the first evidence of endogenous ligands for Piezo channels.
source: A recent study provided the first evidence of endogenous ligands for Piezo channels (Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Sugisawa study.

claim: It was shown that Piezo1 functions as a ligand-gated ion channel to sense single-stranded RNAs (ssRNAs).
source: Remarkably, it was shown that Piezo1 functions as a ligand-gated ion channel to sense single-stranded RNAs (ssRNAs).
evidence: This refers to the findings from the Sugisawa study that the authors are attempting to replicate.

claim: It was proposed that bioactive ssRNAs are produced by the gut microbiome and function through Piezo1 channels to alter serotonin production and trigger a physiological cascade that impacts bone homeostasis.
source: It was proposed that bioactive ssRNAs are produced by the gut microbiome, and that these molecules function through Piezo1 channels to alter serotonin production and trigger a physiological cascade that impacts bone homeostasis.
evidence: This refers to the hypothesis from the Sugisawa study.

claim: ssRNA40 is a synthetic 20-mer ssRNA oligonucleotide derived from the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) genome.
source: ssRNA40 is a synthetic 20-mer ssRNA oligonucleotide derived from the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) genome (Heil et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original characterization of ssRNA40.

claim: ssRNA40 is an agonist for the immune surveillance toll-like receptors 7 and 8 in mice and humans, respectively.
source: ssRNA40 is classically known as an agonist for the immune surveillance toll-like receptors 7 and 8 in mice and humans, respectively (Heil et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It was recently reported that ssRNA40 shows agonist activity toward the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1.
source: However, it was recently reported that ssRNA40 also shows agonist activity toward the mechanosensitive ion channel Piezo1 (Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This refers to findings from the Sugisawa study.

claim: N2a cells natively express Piezo1.
source: To test this finding, we first used the Neuro-2a (N2a) mouse neuroblastoma cell line since these cells natively express Piezo1 (Coste et al., 2010) and were reported to conduct a Piezo1-dependent current in the presence of ssRNA40 (Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: N2a cells were reported to conduct a Piezo1-dependent current in the presence of ssRNA40.
source: To test this finding, we first used the Neuro-2a (N2a) mouse neuroblastoma cell line since these cells natively express Piezo1 (Coste et al., 2010) and were reported to conduct a Piezo1-dependent current in the presence of ssRNA40 (Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This refers to findings from the Sugisawa study.

claim: Application of ssRNA40 did not elicit a detectable increase in fluorescence in N2a cells.
source: Using ssRNA40 from the same supplier and dosage as prior studies (10 µg/mL) (Sugisawa et al., 2020), we found that application of ssRNA40 did not elicit a detectable increase in fluorescence, even when the imaging time frame was extended up to 3 min (Figure 1A and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Yoda1 is known to induce Piezo1-dependent calcium transients.
source: As a positive control for Piezo1 activation, we used Yoda1, which is known to induce Piezo1-dependent calcium transients (Syeda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: 30 µM Yoda1 triggered a dramatic calcium influx over the course of ~1 min in virtually all N2a cells.
source: A 30 µM Yoda1 triggered a dramatic calcium influx over the course of ~1 min in virtually all N2a cells (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: ssRNA41 is the same length and sequence as ssRNA40, except all uridine residues are substituted with adenosine.
source: ssRNA41 is the same length and sequence as ssRNA40, except all uridine residues are substituted with adenosine; unlike ssRNA40, this molecule is not a TLR7/8 agonist (Heil et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original characterization.

claim: ssRNA41 is not a TLR7/8 agonist.
source: ssRNA41 is the same length and sequence as ssRNA40, except all uridine residues are substituted with adenosine; unlike ssRNA40, this molecule is not a TLR7/8 agonist (Heil et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original characterization.

claim: There was no significant difference in N2a cell calcium activity between vehicle controls and ssRNA40.
source: After autofluorescence subtraction, there was no significant difference in N2a cell calcium activity between these negative controls and ssRNA40 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ssRNA40 was reported to delay the inactivation of Piezo1 mechanically evoked currents.
source: In addition to directly activating Piezo1, ssRNA40 was reported to delay the inactivation of Piezo1 mechanically evoked currents (Sugisawa et al., 2020), similar to Yoda1 (Syeda et al., 2015).
evidence: This refers to findings from the Sugisawa study.

claim: Yoda1 delays the inactivation of Piezo1 mechanically evoked currents.
source: In addition to directly activating Piezo1, ssRNA40 was reported to delay the inactivation of Piezo1 mechanically evoked currents (Sugisawa et al., 2020), similar to Yoda1 (Syeda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Mechanical stimulation of N2a cells elicited a rapidly inactivating inward current, which is characteristic of the Piezo family of ion channels.
source: The stimulation elicited a rapidly inactivating inward current, which is characteristic of the Piezo family of ion channels (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1D and established knowledge about Piezo channels.

claim: 30 µM Yoda1 in the external bath solution resulted in a reduced apparent mechanical activation threshold and a prolonged inactivation phase of the currents in N2a cells.
source: As expected, including 30 µM Yoda1 in the external bath solution resulted in a reduced apparent mechanical activation threshold and a prolonged inactivation phase of the currents (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: 10 µg/mL ssRNA40 in the bath solution showed no measurable change from the vehicle control on the amplitude, activation threshold, or inactivation rate of mechanically evoked currents in N2a cells.
source: By contrast, 10 µg/mL ssRNA40 in the bath solution showed no measurable change from the vehicle control on the amplitude, activation threshold, or inactivation rate of mechanically evoked currents (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: ssRNA40 was reported to have a relatively small effect size compared to the Piezo1 agonist activity of Yoda1.
source: Compared to the Piezo1 agonist activity of Yoda1, ssRNA40 was reported to have a relatively small effect size (Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This refers to findings from the Sugisawa study.

claim: HEK293 cells express very low but detectable levels of human Piezo1.
source: There was a noticeable but nonsignificant calcium response of untransfected cells to Yoda1 (Figure 2C), consistent with a previous report that HEK293 cells express very low but detectable levels of human Piezo1 (Dubin et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research and data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In both untransfected and Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells, there was no significant calcium activity between vehicle, ssRNA40, and ssRNA41.
source: However, in both untransfected and Piezo1-transfected conditions, we found no significant calcium activity between vehicle, ssRNA40, and ssRNA41 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Prior studies used between 5 and 20 µg/mL ssRNA40 in their experiments.
source: Prior studies used between 5 and 20 µg/mL ssRNA40 in their experiments (Heil et al., 2004; Lehmann et al., 2012; Shibata et al., 2016; Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ssRNA40 did not trigger significant calcium influx in Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells at any concentration from 0.05 to 50 µg/mL.
source: Using a log scale range from 0.05 to 50 µg/mL, we did not observe significant calcium influx triggered by ssRNA40 at any concentration (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The Piezo1-KO HEK293 cell line used in this study is the identical cell line used in the originally published ssRNA experiments on Piezo1.
source: Importantly, this is the identical cell line used in the originally published ssRNA experiments on Piezo1 (Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Sugisawa study.

claim: No increase in calcium was detected in PIEZO1-KO HEK293 cells throughout exposure to ssRNA40, and there were no significant differences between transfected and untransfected cells or across the various ssRNA40 concentrations.
source: No increase in calcium was detected throughout exposure to ssRNA40, and there were no significant differences between transfected and untransfected cells or across the various ssRNA40 concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FLIPR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no change in the Yoda1 response following treatment with vehicle or different ssRNA40 concentrations in PIEZO1-KO HEK293 cells.
source: However, we found no change in the Yoda1 response following treatment with vehicle or different ssRNA40 concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by FLIPR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ssRNA40 does not activate Piezo1 directly or modulate its mechanotransduction in either N2a cells or HEK293 cells.
source: Together, these data independently corroborate our previous observations that ssRNA40 does not activate Piezo1 directly or modulate its mechanotransduction in either N2a cells or HEK293 cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined negative results from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Both crude fecal extracts and purified fecal RNA were reported to elicit a calcium influx in Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells.
source: It was reported that both crude fecal extracts and purified fecal RNA elicit a calcium influx in Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells (Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This refers to findings from the Sugisawa study.

claim: Applying fecal extract to Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells triggered a substantial calcium response.
source: Applying fecal extract to Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells triggered a substantial calcium response (Figure 3A and Video 3).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The response to 5 mg/mL fecal extract was variable; not all cells in the field of view would necessarily respond, and the response onset was often 30–60 s after the fecal extract was first added.
source: Interestingly, across several imaging trials, we noticed that the response to 5 mg/mL fecal extract was variable; not all cells in the field of view would necessarily respond, and the response onset was often 30–60 s after the fecal extract was first added (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Untransfected HEK293 cells had a similar calcium response to fecal extract as Piezo1-transfected cells.
source: Notably, however, we also found that untransfected HEK293 cells had a similar calcium response to fecal extract, suggesting that fecal extracts may trigger calcium influx via a Piezo1-independent mechanism (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Fecal extracts trigger calcium influx via a Piezo1-independent mechanism.
source: Notably, however, we also found that untransfected HEK293 cells had a similar calcium response to fecal extract, suggesting that fecal extracts may trigger calcium influx via a Piezo1-independent mechanism (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that untransfected cells respond similarly to transfected cells.

claim: Piezo1-KO HEK293 cells responded to fecal extract despite the complete absence of Piezo1.
source: This was confirmed by applying fecal extract to Piezo1-KO HEK293 cells, which still responded despite the complete absence of Piezo1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Purified fecal RNA at 10 µg/mL did not induce a detectable calcium influx in Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells.
source: In contrast to the total extract, we did not observe a detectable calcium influx with 10 µg/mL fecal RNA – the same concentration used in other studies (Figure 3D; Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both RNase-treated and untreated fecal extracts activated Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells to a similar degree.
source: Both RNase-treated and untreated fecal extracts activated Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells to a similar degree (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Fecal extracts can stimulate calcium influx in HEK293 cells, but this effect is unlikely to be mediated by RNA and does not depend on Piezo1.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrate that fecal extracts can stimulate calcium influx in HEK293 cells, but this effect is unlikely to be mediated by RNA and, regardless, the activity does not depend on Piezo1.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the RNase treatment and Piezo1-KO experiments.

claim: Applying 5 mg/mL dietary extract to HEK293 cells produced a substantial calcium response.
source: Surprisingly, applying 5 mg/mL dietary extract to HEK293 cells produced a substantial calcium response (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Dietary extract activation occurred in both untransfected and Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells.
source: This activation occurred in both untransfected and Piezo1-transfected cells.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Dietary extract often activated only a subset of HEK293 cells.
source: Similar to fecal extract, the dietary extract often activated only a subset of cells (Figure 3E and Video 4).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The timing of the response onset to dietary extract was variable but tended to occur earlier compared to fecal extract.
source: The timing of the response onset was also variable but tended to occur earlier compared to fecal extract (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Dietary extract activated Piezo1-KO HEK293 cells, confirming that Piezo1 is dispensable for the response to the extract.
source: Dietary extract also activated Piezo1-KO HEK293 cells, confirming that Piezo1 is dispensable for the response to the extract (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The osmolality and pH of fecal and dietary extracts were not substantially altered compared to control Ringer's solution.
source: To verify that the dietary and fecal extracts were not activating cells in a nonspecific way by changing the osmolality or pH, we confirmed that these properties were not substantially altered between control solutions and the crude extracts (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by measurements described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: An element of the mouse diet, if present in fecal matter, could be a confounding factor when studying active compounds derived from the host gut or resident microbiota in calcium imaging assays.
source: These results suggest that an element of the mouse diet, if present in fecal matter, could be a confounding factor when studying active compounds derived from the host gut or resident microbiota in calcium imaging assays.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dietary extracts activate cells similarly to fecal extracts.

claim: Piezo1 is a nonselective ion channel that inactivates quickly (within 10–30 ms).
source: Piezo1 is a nonselective ion channel that inactivates quickly (within 10–30 ms) (Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: The maximum whole-cell Piezo1 current evoked by mechanical stimulation was not substantially different across vehicle, ssRNA40, fecal extract, and Yoda1 conditions.
source: Across all conditions, the maximum whole-cell Piezo1 current evoked by mechanical stimulation was not substantially different.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Yoda1 significantly lowered the apparent mechanical threshold for Piezo1 activation and delayed channel inactivation in Piezo1-transfected HEK293 cells.
source: By contrast, Yoda1 significantly lowered the apparent mechanical threshold for Piezo1 activation and delayed channel inactivation as expected (Figure 4B and C; Syeda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4B and C and citation to prior research.

claim: The results do not provide evidence for even a limited effect of either ssRNA40 or fecal extracts on the biophysical properties of Piezo1.
source: Together, our results do not provide evidence for even a limited effect of either ssRNA40 or fecal extracts on the biophysical properties of Piezo1.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the electrophysiology data showing no changes in Piezo1 properties.

claim: Piezo1 was originally discovered in N2a cells.
source: Piezo1 was originally discovered in N2a cells (Coste et al., 2010), and this cell line continues to be frequently used for in vitro work on Piezo1 (Geng et al., 2020; Ridone et al., 2020; Romero et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: N2a cells continue to be frequently used for in vitro work on Piezo1.
source: Piezo1 was originally discovered in N2a cells (Coste et al., 2010), and this cell line continues to be frequently used for in vitro work on Piezo1 (Geng et al., 2020; Ridone et al., 2020; Romero et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research using N2a cells.

claim: Untransfected N2a Piezo1-KO cells showed no calcium response to Yoda1 treatment, confirming an absence of Piezo1.
source: The untransfected N2a Piezo1-KO cells showed no calcium response to Yoda1 treatment, confirming an absence of Piezo1 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: N2a Piezo1-KO cells that were transfected with Piezo1 showed a large calcium response to Yoda1, confirming an efficient transfection.
source: Conversely, N2a Piezo1-KO cells that were transfected with Piezo1 showed a large calcium response to Yoda1, confirming an efficient transfection.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Unlike HEK293 cells, N2a cells did not respond to either fecal or dietary extracts.
source: Interestingly, unlike HEK293 cells, N2a cells did not respond to either fecal or dietary extracts (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Piezo1 transfection did not endow N2a cells with sensitivity to fecal or dietary extracts.
source: Moreover, Piezo1 transfection did not endow N2a cells with sensitivity to either of these extracts (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Neither fecal extracts nor RNA derived from the gut microbiome can activate Piezo1.
source: From these data, we conclude that neither fecal extracts nor RNA derived from the gut microbiome can activate Piezo1.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined negative results from multiple cell lines and experimental approaches.

claim: Fecal/dietary extract sensitivity appears to be linked to other cell line-specific factors found in HEK293 cells but not N2a cells.
source: Instead, fecal/dietary extract sensitivity appears to be linked to other cell line-specific factors found in HEK293 cells but not N2a cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential responses between HEK293 and N2a cells.

claim: RIN14B is a pancreatic endocrine cell line commonly used to model gut enterochromaffin cell function.
source: This pancreatic endocrine cell line is commonly used to model gut enterochromaffin cell function and natively expresses Piezo1 (Nozawa et al., 2009; Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RIN14B cells natively express Piezo1.
source: This pancreatic endocrine cell line is commonly used to model gut enterochromaffin cell function and natively expresses Piezo1 (Nozawa et al., 2009; Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ssRNA40 and ssRNA41 elicited a noticeable calcium response in RIN14B cells.
source: However, ssRNA40 and ssRNA41 elicited a noticeable calcium response in RIN14B cells, unlike in N2a or HEK293 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fecal RNA elicited a calcium response in RIN14B cells, similar in magnitude to that caused by ssRNA40 and ssRNA41.
source: Fecal RNA also elicited a calcium response, similar in magnitude to that caused by ssRNA40 and ssRNA41 (Figure 6D-F and Video 5).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Yoda1 led to a significantly larger increase in fluorescence in RIN14B cells compared to ssRNA40, ssRNA41, and fecal RNA.
source: In comparison, Yoda1 led to a significantly larger increase in fluorescence, consistent with endogenous expression of Piezo1 in RIN14B cells (Figure 6G-I).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6G-I.

claim: Gadolinium is a broad inhibitor of stretch-activated cation channels including Piezo1.
source: Gadolinium is a broad inhibitor of stretch-activated cation channels including Piezo1 (Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Gadolinium reduced spontaneous calcium transients in RIN14B cells during vehicle application.
source: At baseline, we noticed general effects of gadolinium on the excitability of RIN14B cells, evident by reduced spontaneous calcium transients during vehicle application (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Gadolinium did not diminish the response to fecal RNA in RIN14B cells.
source: Notably, gadolinium did not diminish the response to fecal RNA, but it seemed to have a nonspecific effect on the decay rate of the calcium signal (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Gadolinium completely abolished the Yoda1 response in RIN14B cells, confirming successful Piezo1 inhibition.
source: Gadolinium completely abolished the Yoda1 response, confirming successful Piezo1 inhibition (Figure 6H and I).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6H and I.

claim: RIN14B cells respond to a variety of ssRNAs, but their response is not dependent on Piezo1.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrate that while RIN14B cells do respond to a variety of ssRNAs, their response is not dependent on Piezo1.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the gadolinium inhibition experiments.

claim: RIN14B cells and gut enterochromaffin cells express the electrophile receptor Trpa1.
source: In addition to Piezo1, RIN14B cells and gut enterochromaffin cells express the electrophile receptor Trpa1 (Bellono et al., 2017; Nozawa et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Trpa1 has been reported to respond to extracellular microRNAs.
source: We speculated that Trpa1 may be responsible for the RNA-induced calcium response, considering that Trpa1 has been reported to respond to extracellular microRNAs (Park et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The Trpa1 inhibitor A-967079 blocked the calcium response following addition of allyl isothiocyanate (AITC) in RIN14B cells.
source: As expected, the Trpa1 inhibitor blocked the calcium response following addition of allyl isothiocyanate (AITC), an electrophilic Trpa1 agonist (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Trpa1 inhibitor did not significantly diminish the calcium response following addition of ssRNA40 or ssRNA41 in RIN14B cells.
source: However, the Trpa1 inhibitor did not significantly diminish the calcium response following addition of ssRNA40 or ssRNA41 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that the RNA-induced response is not dependent on Trpa1.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The RNA-induced response in RIN14B cells is not dependent on Trpa1.
source: However, the Trpa1 inhibitor did not significantly diminish the calcium response following addition of ssRNA40 or ssRNA41 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that the RNA-induced response is not dependent on Trpa1.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of Trpa1 inhibition on ssRNA responses.

claim: Algorithmic clustering of individual nuclear transcriptomes from RIN14B cells did not reveal any clear transcriptomic subpopulations.
source: Algorithmic clustering of individual nuclear transcriptomes did not reveal any clear transcriptomic subpopulations.
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-nuclei RNA sequencing data.

claim: There is heterogeneity in the prevalence of individual transcripts from cell to cell in RIN14B cells.
source: However, there is clearly heterogeneity when examining the prevalence of individual transcripts from cell to cell, which may stem from true biological heterogeneity within the cell line or from technical limitations in our sequencing approach (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of single-nuclei RNA sequencing data.

claim: The authors were not able to detect ssRNA-evoked changes in Piezo1 activity with in vitro calcium imaging and electrophysiological recordings.
source: In this study, we set out to confirm the discovery that Piezo1 is a sensor of fecal microbiome ssRNA. We were not able to detect ssRNA-evoked changes in Piezo1 activity with in vitro calcium imaging and electrophysiological recordings.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on all the negative results presented in the study.

claim: ssRNAs and fecal extracts can stimulate calcium influx in cultured cells, but this calcium activity depends on the cell line being used, rather than Piezo1 function.
source: Instead, we present evidence that ssRNAs and fecal extracts can stimulate calcium influx in cultured cells, but this calcium activity depends on the cell line being used, rather than Piezo1 function.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the differential responses observed across different cell lines.

claim: Dietary extracts can elicit calcium influx similar to fecal extracts.
source: An unexpected finding is that dietary extracts can elicit calcium influx similar to fecal extracts.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data comparing dietary and fecal extracts.

claim: Different mouse colonies in different facilities showed differential effects of fecal/dietary extracts, with some preparations showing more or less activity.
source: We also observed differential effects of fecal/dietary extracts between mouse colonies in different facilities, with some preparations showing more or less activity.
evidence: This is based on comparing extracts prepared from mice at NIH versus Scripps/HHMI.

claim: It is important to control for elements of the diet when working with gut-derived samples.
source: This highlights the importance of controlling for elements of the diet when working with gut-derived samples.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dietary extracts can confound results.

claim: The observation that the enterochromaffin model cell line RIN14B responds to ssRNAs corroborates recent evidence that there exists a gut-resident RNA receptor.
source: Interestingly, our observation that the enterochromaffin model cell line RIN14B responds to ssRNAs corroborates the recent evidence that there exists a gut-resident RNA receptor (Sugisawa et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on the RIN14B calcium imaging data and citation to the Sugisawa study.

claim: The authors are unable to reproduce the finding that Piezo1 is an RNA receptor.
source: However, we are unable to reproduce the finding that Piezo1 is an RNA receptor, and we propose that Piezo1 is more likely functioning as a mechanosensor in the gut, as has been shown in many other tissues (Murthy et al., 2017; Syeda, 2021; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on all the negative results presented in the study.

claim: Piezo1 is more likely functioning as a mechanosensor in the gut, as has been shown in many other tissues.
source: However, we are unable to reproduce the finding that Piezo1 is an RNA receptor, and we propose that Piezo1 is more likely functioning as a mechanosensor in the gut, as has been shown in many other tissues (Murthy et al., 2017; Syeda, 2021; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the authors' negative results and citations to prior research on Piezo1 mechanosensing.
